blocks.x: You don't understand? No, I never did learn French. If you could tell us your name first
or we'll have it on the tape. Right now? Yes. You want my name now? Yes. Well, in English, eh? Yes. Well, my name is Alice, my maiden name you want? Yeah, that'd be good too. Your maiden
name and then your... Alice William Zeno. And your married name was Zeno. Yes,

you know, Louis Zeno. Henry Louis Zeno was my married name. And my maiden name was Alice William. Can you tell us how old you are now? Well, now I'll be 94 years old in four months, five months from now. 95? Eh? 95 and five. 94. I'm 94 now. 94 now. Yeah. Where were you born? Right on in the city or outside? I was born on St. Claude Street between Calarack and Columbus. Right here in this city. Well, this is not the city. Yes. Over there. I still think I'm over there too.
St. Claude Street, you know? Your birthday? The 7th of June. I remembered that. I wanted to get it on here.
Yeah. The 7th of June, what year was that? In 1864. 1864. See? When? In 1864. I see.
I see. Maybe not a fire. Was the war around then? You wouldn't remember, I mean, do you remember when the war was over?

The war was over. About April, wasn't it? Yes. The war was over, you know, everything was all right, settled for the month of April. And I was born in the month of June. Yeah, that's what I thought. It was just about three months, four months, three months after everything was settled.
Can I see?
Can you remember your parents and your grandmother too? You told me about your grandmother once.
If I remember my grandmother, oh Lord, yes. If I remember my grandmother. Seems like she's right in front of me now. And I miss her. I miss her. She was 101 years and 15 days when she died.
101. Well, you may make that too.
Oh, Mr. Russell.
I hope you do.
No, no, I don't hope that.
Well, if you're well, unless you're well, there's no need to live. Yes, if I was well. But you look well.
When did your grandmother die?
She died on the 15th day of January. And she was 101 year on the 1st of January. She died 101 year and 15 days.
She died in 1910.
Eh?
1910, is all it says.
Was it?
1910, yes. You remember her then real well. Yes, I remember her well.
You told me once that she taught you some Senegalese, the African language, a few words.

Because I used to be right by her all the time. I idolized my grandmother. And she spoke her mother's language. But my mother and my aunt and them, they didn't want her yet that. But me, I would be right there by her. And I tell her, Gagan, because I didn't call her grandma, I called her Gagan. I say, Gagan, tell me, tell me. And she would tell me. And sometimes she'd say, Abadra. Abadra, that means good for nothing. That's Senegal.
What was good morning? You told me that, I think, once.
Salicum Serum. Salicum Serum is good morning, everybody.
Salicum Serum. Another thing I was wondering about, these folks that you worked for once up at Newcomb College came down to get a recipe of that pudding that they made.
Oh, yes. But the poor man died 15 days after I had seen him. And he never come back to get any more.
What kind of a pudding was that? That hasn't maybe anything to do with our music, but I was interested. I wondered though. Just... The pudding. What was it made out of?

That kind of pudding was pepper tart. Potato...not potato pudding, no. It's just like potato pudding, but it's grated, you know. And you've got to put black pepper in there. A good deal of black pepper. Mm-hmm. Pepper tart, they call it.
Anything else much? Something about sugar to make it sweet, of course.
Sugar and eggs. Mm-hmm. And... Milk. Milk.
Milk.
Milk.
Yeah. Milk.
Milk. Yes, milk. And pas du beurre. No butter.
And do you bake it in an oven or put it on top of the stove?
Yeah, in oven, close, you know.
And then just ordinary potato, white potato, not sweet potato. Sweet potato. Sweet potato. Sweet potato.
Oh, yes, sweet potato.
Oh, I didn't get that.
Sweet potato. Sweet potato. Not Irish potato, no. Sweet potato. Sweet potato. It was called pain patate.
And they had that in Africa then, too. Oh, that's the food. Yes, oh, yes.
Well, how much potato do you use?
Well, it depends on the size you want to make, you know.
Well, George can make it then, too. Yeah, maybe, yeah. I just make it. Some day we'll come over. Yeah, George ought to know how.

Because I used... You know me, I like to cook. Mm-hmm. That's why I fuss with George all the time. George don't want me to cook. He don't want me to do nothing. I'm 94, but I'm not crippled. I look like crippled.
No, you look well. Healthy.
I just can't get about fast like I used to be, what you call, so fast and everything. But now, of course, I have to take my time. I'll balance it like this. Mm-hmm. And do. Makes me so mad.
Were any of your family musicians, that is your grandfather or father, did they play anything or sing music?

Oh, nothing I know of. No, my father was a cigar maker. Cigar maker. Mm-hmm. And my grandfather, I never knew him. Yeah. But I remember my grandmother good. Just like I was looking at you. Oh, I wish she was here.
What did she sing, your grandmother?
Did she sing around the house like you do? Any little songs?
Oh, sometimes she'd sing, but I don't remember it.
Mm-hmm.

She was too busy. She had so many grandchildren, you know. Yes. And she took such interest in her children. Oh, she took interest in explaining you things and showing you things and telling you about the weather. When it was going to, the weather was going to change, she was just like a good astronomer. She could tell you. You know, we all washed, my parents, my mother and aunts and them, and she'd come and look up, and she'd say, you all can make your starch today. But, the moment, but look at the weather. Make your starch. Then she'd look up. She'd say, by six hour, we'll have an embelli. Embelli means, you know, the weather changing.
I was interested to know how you learned all of the different languages you speak, where you went to school first, and then how you learned your French and German and all?

Well, French, I learned the French, you see, with the people my mother, when I was born, my mother was working, and as soon as she could go back on the job, she took me and the Miss Mazzaro. They had me in the house like a child, a white child. They didn't want my mother to have anything to do with me. And they spoke nothing but French to me.
Your name was Thoreau?
Mazzaro.
Mazzaro.
Mazzaro.
I see.

And I was fully four, five years that I spoke nothing but French. I didn't know nothing, no Creole, no other language but French. That's how I got it so, so good. And I kept on with the Frenchmen, kept on, because I liked French. Then I worked with the Gascon too.
Wow.
When did you learn German? You said you learned German and Spanish too, didn't you?
Well, that was from Mrs. W. W. King, you know, yes. Grace King's folks? Grace King, Grace Elizabeth King.
Where did she live when you worked for her?
Well, when I went there, they lived on the rampart between Common and Canap. Canap, right.
Canap Street. But her Elks place is along in the...
Oh, yes. They had Mrs. TJ Samms cross the street, Mrs. McCall, Mrs. Morris. But all them people moved, you know, uptown because the neighborhood had gotten to be so bad.
Now, what kind of work did you do when you worked for them? Did you cook for them?

No, no. I was housegirl and maid for Miss Nina King. Yes. Nina's the youngest one. I don't know if she's alive. I know Miss Annie died. But Miss Nina was a debutante then. And I was homemade and did the upstairs work.
We'll have to play this for Dick King. He's related to them. Oh. And ask him about it. He'll enjoy it. I know a relative of Miss King's family.
Of Miss who?
Miss King's.
A relative of Miss King?
Yes. We'll have to play this for him. He'll enjoy hearing about the family. You probably know things that nobody else remembers.
Well, you know Miss King was a Miss Miller.
Oh, I see.

Tom Miller. She had two brothers, Henry and Tom Miller. And Mr. Tom had three children, Miss Grace and Tom and Annie. And they were called Grace King Miller. Oh, yes. I've heard that name. I'm wondering if you... And George, the judge then, Fred.
You told me about the people, this lady that you worked for at Tulane or Newcomb College. One time she found you reading some books she didn't like.
That was Mrs. King.
Oh, was that who it was? I thought it was the other people.
No, no. That was Mrs. King. Oh.
And you read how many languages? Un peu.
Comme ci, comme ça. I understand pretty good. And in French?
In French.

In French. In French. Well, you see, when I was working at Mrs. King, they had...it wasn't a school. It was just like you're nice, convoicing you. Yes. They had Mr. Chaffray. You must have heard of that name, Chaffray? I'm not sure.
Maybe.

And then they had Mrs. Lodoux and Mrs. C.J. Sam's and all. And they speak. Well, that day, that day, that day was just like conversion, it was as if it was French. They had an old lady they called Madame Gérard. She was French. And Charles Gaiary.
Oh, yes. He's a famous man, a historian.
Charles Gaiary.
Very famous man.
You knew your...
I've read his books.

Well, it was nothing but French. And then the next day, it was maybe the Spanish class. Well, that was Capitano Chivarillo. Nothing but Spanish. Nothing. They speak to me in Spanish, the language of the class that was going on. And Herman Gessner. Herman Gessner teaches. That must be his grandson that is teaching at Tulane. Yes, I've heard that name. Yes, Herman Gessner. Well, then him, he was Spanish, German. And nothing but German. They called me and they speak to me in German and asked me things in German. No other language but the language of that day.
So you had to learn all of those languages too?

Well, you know, young, I was young and foolish at last. And one day, Miss Gracie told me, Harps is fee. You have an opportunity of learning things that you will never be able to pay for. And you're there giggling and giggling. And after a while, I said, well, I think Miss Gracie is right. Let me stop giggling and pay attention to what... What I...the opportunity that I had. So there's where I began to catch on. A little German. A little Spanish. Well, I knew French well.
When did you learn English? When did you learn English? Well, with everybody.
Did your folks speak English? Your mother and two years?
No, no, no. My grandmother didn't speak English at all.
How much your mother? Eh? How much your mother? Did your mother though too? Did she speak English?
Oh, and my mother spoke a little English, you know. But her real language was Creole and French.

Would you rather speak French even now? Would you? Today? Oh, now? Oh, yes. Somebody, either George or you, or somebody told me once that you think in French. I don't know how that works exactly because I only know English. But do you, when you think of things, does the French go through your head? French, French.

But sometimes, some things I can't bring out in English. And when I get to fussing with him and he make me mad, I take my French. French. And he just looks at me and laughs. He ought to speak French. Because I spoke French to him all his babyhood. My Sydney, my nephew that I raised from the age of 10 days. And all, all, I spoke French to them. Creole. But they took that English.
Yes, well everybody around now has to have the English, so.
But when they make me mad, I take. I take my language. To conan, to conan, to conan, to conan.
So, you spoke English when you were five years old? No, I spoke nothing but French. And when did you start English? Nothing but French.
Well, after I grew, you know. After you got grown.
After you got grown.

Playing with other children. But most of the time I was of good size. I spoke, I speak French to them. They speak Creole to me. I understood it, but I didn't speak it. It's just after I grew older and older and children, that I began to. But I always did prefer French.
Did you know any little songs, French songs or folk songs when you were young? Do you remember any of those songs you heard?
Well, I was just telling George, I said, George, as many as I knew. I just can't remember nothing. Now, I can remember, but that's not French. It's, uh, how is Jamaican? Jamaica. Jamaica?
Uh-huh.
Jamaican.
That's, uh, Jamaica. You told me.
In Haiti, from Haiti. From Haiti? Haiti. Well, that's a Creole. That's a Creole.
That's Creole. What? Haiti.
Haiti is Creole?
They have a Creole down there. Haiti?

Uh-huh. Yes, I believe it is, because I'll tell you, the French song that I know is mostly mixed up. Uh-huh. Toe tae is siens, dee puis plus dee en zan, tapez, we'll tapez, we'll that's Creole. Uh-huh. Tapez soufer de la plus grande misère, mangez tes chers, pas tes gagnants l'argent, that's Creole. Uh-huh. La peinte est tuée, déjà beaucoup de merde, that's Creole. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
And what is that song about?

Well, it was when they had the revolution in Haiti, Haiti as they call it. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And they had Prince Geoffrey, and he had to come to do for them, you know, to help them out, because they were starving. Starving. The mothers were starving. You notice, they say, la feinte, la feinte est tuée, la feinte est tuée, that means hunger kills the many mothers. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh.
And do you know any other songs that you remember from way back? Uh-huh. It's hard for me to bring them.
You told me last year that sometime you sing to yourself when you're working around the house to keep from being lonesome.

When I was young, that's all I passed my time in. And work hard, hard, hard. I did nothing but shirts for Mr. Villere and all them people, shirts only. And I'd have the yard lined with shirts. All day the lady next door, they sewed, and they used to put their machine by the window to hear me sing. Uh-huh. And all day long, and one day one of the ladies says, but at least I always hear you say, oh, I'm hungry. I never hear you sound tired. I say, well, I'm never tired. Sing, sing, sing, sing, sing, sing all day.
That kept you from getting tired?
Well, I don't know what was, but I just loved to sing then.
Did you sing songs about being hungry?
No. No, I didn't. I'd sing just what would come to my mind, but I'd sing. Work like a little horse, like a machine.
Is El Abba an old song or a new song?
No. No.
Sir? Do you know that song, El Abba, El Abba? Is that new or old?
El Abba. Mm-hmm.
Some of the bands play it, even George's band plays it, and the slow drag. Sing it, you know better songs than any of us.
Slow drag sings it usually. You know the words?
El Abba means hey over there. That's Creole. You know Mo Palais Mesa?
That's a carnival song. Mo Palais Mesa, Mo Palais Mesa.
You see I can't get that together. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . That's a carnival song. Yeah, carnival song .
Yeah .
Carnival, huh?
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Oh, different carnival than now. Oh, it was really lively, worth following. Because I have a cousin just died, that he did a year, eh?
Just about a year.
Well, he was one of them. He had been, about six or sometimes 12 of them. And they would go around, they dressed in women, and they'd sing, and they'd sing.
And did Tati play music?

No, he'd mass. Oh, but he'd... Massive. Lively, lively. Whenever you'd hear that, they could say that people would run, you know, those old folks, even those that was busy, that they would run. Here comes Tati's band. He was very, very, very lively. Oh, he made a good, good Mardi Gras.
Do you know a song called, Como Té Piti?
Como Té Piti? Mm-hmm. I don't remember that.
What about, uh... Les Ognons?
Les Ognons. You know that song? Les Ognons sont à Beaumarché. Oui.
Les Ognons.
C'est les ci, c'est les ça. Ma con-mère tourne le dos. Mm-hmm.
Well, the church used to use that when they were, uh...
Eh?
Played Ring Around. Ring Around.

Oh, that goes with Ring Around the Road. Yeah, that was, you'd hold hands together. Yeah. And all the children, you know, around the neighborhood, children wasn't studying about that one like they do now. They all play Ring Around. Les Ognons. Mm-hmm. Eh... Comment y'appelle les autres chansons Ring Around, là?
Are there any of the songs you sing today and nowadays when you work? What do you sing now? I don't know more. You sing now. I sing now.
Sometimes, sometimes... When I see George look down, you know, then... If something come, then I begin to sing it. Cheer him up.
Mm-hmm. Could you sing a part of a little song like that or even hum it right now to see what it's

like? Sing all kinds. Anything would come to my mind then. Anything. Ah, yes. It was the good old days. Mm-hmm. We think we have it hard now. No, no. Those were the better days. Do you know a song of... I'm going to add it on the tip of my tongue. Mademoiselle Josephine, something a la Rudolphine? I can't think.
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm .

Mm-hmm . I think I've heard that myself, but I don't know if it was Ori or what. Blanche Tukat is one Ori sings. Yeah, Blanche Tukat, yeah. It was another one, wasn't it? Yeah, he had one called, the play sings, A La Pa, and one called Creole Boba, which is the same tune as Twinkle Twinkle Little Star. Remember that bit? Oh yeah. Do you know Twinkle Twinkle Little Star? The song in English is Twinkle Twinkle? No. Can you whistle that for our knowledge? Yeah. With the hat? Yeah. Yeah.
That's it, eh? Yeah. Up above the moon so high, up above the world so high. The world so high. Like a diamond in the sky.

Like a diamond in the sky. Well, there are Creole words to that that Ori used to sing. In Creole, but it was something different. He called it Creole Boba. I don't know what it is. I didn't understand it.
I don't know no Creole song.

Me, myself, I don't know. Even so, I didn't know I couldn't sing when I was singing. But, uh… Did they ever sing at weddings? No. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Did they ever sing at weddings? Creole songs at weddings? No.

I wonder what kind of music did they have? Did you ever go to any dances when you were young, a little girl even? Did you hear any of the dance music when you were even a child? Oh, yes. We used to… What was the music like? What kind of an orchestra did they have or band? Most of the string band.
String band.
Violin, carnet.
Mm-hmm. But most of the… Like… Accordion. Accordion. Accordion. Accordion. Accordion. Mm-hmm. And bass. And bass.
Bass violins, yeah. Did they have any drums or triangles or anything like that?
I don't remember they had drums when I was going out.
Anything like George's clarinet or a flute or anything like that?
Well, they'd have flutes, yes. And they'd have violin and they'd have bass. Piccolos.
And horn, well, they'd have cornet.
Yeah.
Would they have slide trombones in those days or valve trombones?
I never noticed that, but I know they'd have cornet.
Cornet. Do you remember anything about the bands in the Mardi Gras parades? Did they have a brass band or what?
Well, in the Mardi Gras parade it was more so a brass band, you know.
Even when you were a child, do you remember that? Oh, well, yes.
Or the... Then it was, they didn't have violin in the parade, no.
I wonder what kind of a band, that was way back. And when you were a child, they did have the brass band that marched with the...
Yes, they didn't have, it was brass band marching.
And what would they play? What instruments?
Well, a cornet and a flute.
I'm sure they'd tremble. Eh?
Probably about the same as now, I guess.
Probably about the same as now, I'm sure. Would they have drums?
Oh, yes, they'd have drums.
And the cymbals? Yeah. Would they have cymbals like this? Or would they hit... Big drum? I think they would.
And this, what's it called? Hand cymbals.
Yeah. Hand cymbals. And now today, they put the cymbals on the bass drum. Uh-huh. And he hits the bass drum with one hand. Did they do that then, do you remember?
No. Well, yes. It began to come, you know, as I grew. Yes. But before it was, they just like this. Just the two, one in each hand.
Yeah.
One in each hand.

Let's see. I'm wondering, the... Before George even was born, what kind of dance music they played. Do you remember any dances you went to way back? What the music was like? Did they play waltzes or... And quadrilles.
Quadrilles. Quadrilles. Oh, it's so long since they don't have quadrilles. Quadrilles was pretty, too. Oh, yes. I've seen one. Yeah.
They revived it.
Quadrilles was pretty.
It was... It wasn't a real one. It was special for television. Quadrilles, it was, let's see, three, four men, two men, eh? And four ladies.

It all pent upon the audience. The public dances, they had as many people as they wanted. Yeah, I guess so. Yeah, they had as many, because I played quadrilles myself with René and Albert Glennie. Oh, yes. Albert Glennie's time it was.
And they had as many people as they wanted to get on the floor. And what kind of music did you play? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And what kind of music could go with the quadrilles? Well, it varied in different tempos. Mm-hmm. Waltzes and falses and... Polka. ...marches. You know, and they'd play so many chords and they'd stop and they'd bow and change and, you know, go around.
The man would take the girl and waltz them to you.
It's almost something like... I don't know a similar to what I call a similar thing.

And you'd have one on each side. And then him, he would dance alone in the middle of the floor. And he'd dance and dance and dance until he'd get... Dan, take one. And he'd waltz back and the other one would do the same, waltz to him. So it's pretty.
Would they dance a mazooka? Yeah, all that went on. Mazooka. Polka. Polka. Polka. All that went on. Shortage. Shortage, yeah. All that went on.
They don't dance polka now? No, I guess not. No. I don't know if that's what you call shortage.
I don't know if shortage is different.
But long time they danced polka in Mazooka.
Shortage was slow. Mm-hmm. Shortage was slow in the walls.
And waltz plenty. Because before the quadrille time, they'd give about two, three quadrilles a knife. But before the quadrille come, they'd play waltz. They'd have waltz all around the hall.
What about lances and varieties? What were they like? Well, that's in quadrilles.
That's part of the quadrilles.
Yeah, the lances and the quadrilles.
That's part of the quadrilles. Yeah, the lances and the quadrilles. Varieties?

What is that like, varieties? Have you ever seen them? Yeah. Lenny used to tell me about it. That's how I... I never knew the name of all of them, but I know I played it with him. I played corpule for bankers, for French later society, you know. And they'd stop a while and then the guy would call out something in Creole, a figure like, and then they'd start again. The music would probably call a variety would be different temples. Maybe I'll just say that. Yeah. Well we'll ask my name Senegal sometime, we'll get her. She called it, remember, on the boat? She called it. We'll get her. But I think it is. Each time she called something, it's something different, you know, in the title of the music. It's slow, it's fast, or it's a bow or something like that.
That's in the quadrilles.
Yeah.
I was wondering about the first kind of music, something like George, you've heard George's band. I guess you don't get around to hear it very much, but you've heard his records. That type of music.
I never have the chance of going where George is playing with the whole band. She just heard the records. I'm wondering when you... Just the records, that's all I heard.
When you were young, did you ever hear any music, something like that, that type of music? No. Like George plays note.
No. It was, they play with music, you see, the note. They used to have read it off of the music. Yes, but now they play by routines. That's what they call jazz, eh? Yes.
Did they ever use the word writing time? In my days, no.
Didn't know what that was.
But when did that word come in?
I don't know when that come in, but in my days they didn't have that right time.
I see. Probably, maybe they had to change the syndrome, not beginning.
Do you remember the first time you heard any of the songs? Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Okay, it's going again. You were talking about Isidore Fritz and different people.

Yeah, I heard because Bunk was supposed to be instructing that band, Isidore Fritz, the old man Fritz, and Loya Fritz, and little Caggley who plays trumpet. B's brother, Kleyber, was playing the drum all this way with Tommy Ladner.
They all came from across the lake today and lived over there.
And where did Tommy Ladner play then?
Tommy Ladner played a while with that Sam Fritz band. Bunk would come over weekends when he was available, you know.
And what instrument was he playing that? Who that? Tommy Ladner. He started on trumpet, you think?
Yeah, that's what he was playing that night. I don't know what he started on, but that's what he was playing.
So many guys change, I want to check.
That's what he was playing.
Was that in Mandeville?
Mandeville, yeah.
What about Covington, what is it, Beda Springs? Did you ever get around there?
I played in Beda Springs, I played in Covington, I played in Unita, Tick Faw, Hammond. All through in that neighborhood.

Well what about the Fritz band? Bunk was instructing them you said? Did they play it before they learned how to read or what? Well I never saw anyone with any music. I'm not telling you. I don't know. Well how did Bunk instruct him then?
Bunk was teaching them, that's all I see.
Yeah, I see.

I never saw any music. I never saw no band use any music except, the first band I saw use music over there was Leonard Parker's band. And then Parker was a good spell a little bit and he used to, I saw him with music. But the rest of them I never saw anyone with no music. And then also René used to come over there with Morris French and Morris French's brother with the tuba, playing the tuba at the different time, used to come over there and they wrote it.
Who was the clarinet player?
Zeb. Zeb. Zeb was playing the clarinet.
And uh...
What style did Zeb play, interrupt again? What kind of a player was Zeb?
Zeb played on the style I played on almost. Just not one part of the same style.
Did you hear Edmund Hall over there?
Yes. I tried to take Edmund Hall, plays with Buddy Petit when Edmund Hall left.
Did he play the same as he plays now? Almost. Almost. Would Zeb have a tone like him or more like yours? Zeb had a tone more like Edmund Hall. What about Georgie Boyd? What kind of tone did he have?
Georgie Boyd had a tone like Edmund Hall too.
Just checking on. Oh, when was the first time you ever heard Bunk to your knowledge?

Well, the first time I heard Bunk was in his twenties. That's the first time I heard Bunk when Bunk was a younger man. I heard Bunk in New Orleans too. I heard Bunk here on Parades. I heard Bunk at Banquets. You know, we called Bunk kids. We called them Bunk kids at the Hopes Hall. I heard him at the – they never gave too many at the Economy Hall. But the Perseverance Hall and the New Hall there and also the – where the big I-Lewy used to stay at Artesian Hall. That's where the Bunk was mostly.

Tell a little bit more about those Bunk kids. They had one at the Union when you were up in Chicago the last time. Dick and I were invited over. But of course there they lined up, you know, and went around and got chicken. It wasn't served to them or anything. But were the old Bunk kids more formal? How did they – what did they do? Have music or what all did they do?

Well, I'll tell you how they did. The organizations would have, say like it would be the anniversary of the society. It would be two years old probably next – this year or three or whatever year, you know – well every year on that date they would have this banquet. Well they'd take – so many members would be of the Catholic faiths, so many would be of the Baptist faiths. But one year they'd go to a Baptist church if it was a Baptist, well they'd go on a Sunday evening, you know, for this service. If it was a Catholic they'd go for Mass in the morning of the day of the banquet. And all the members would get in the line and walk. No music though. We'd meet at the church and they'd walk and they'd come to the hall and they'd have the chocolate and the ham and donuts. And then at a certain time of the day around 12 they'd have the dinner. And at one o'clock the music would start until six. Four, five?
Six, six. Six.
Six. Under six. And then each member would have an invitation. I'd give you an invitation. Sometimes some fellows could get in without invitations, sometimes they couldn't.
Did they have any speeches or other kind of entertainments or after-dinner speeches or dancing later?

No, dancing after the dinner which would be at 12 o'clock. And then the band would start at one. Around about 2, 2.30 and they'd call the band down. Everything was free. They'd feed the band. Yeah, everything was free.
They'd get beer early.

Beer with no bottle beer. It was all cake beer. They'd have big agate pitches. They'd serve it in a lot of pitches. And everybody would have a good time. If it was a children organization, well they'd have beer for the grown people and ice cream and cake for the children and lemonade, you know. They'd have a really, really good time. A lot of times there'd be a lot of fuss about this member went and said he didn't get enough for the money. You know, each member would be taxed so much, but they didn't get enough to eat for their money. They said the committees would take it all and all such things as that. Back to Bunk for a minute.
Yeah, go ahead. I'll get that in my life. Yeah. Now Bunk, his records and his playing during the 40s, how did they compare with the way he played in the 20s?
Well, they didn't compare at all. Bunk played fine on up until Bunk lost his teeth.
So he was better then?
Well, he was much better. I know that for a fact, because I played the last jobs with Bunk, and Bunk had his teeth, so I know that for a fact.
Yeah.

Because after Evan Thomas got killed, Bunk taking the job over, we had a couple of jobs to play, and we only used one trumpet. The Bunk was playing fine, but after he lost his teeth and had laid off for that many years, and ten years made him ten years older. That would make some difference. That would make a lot of difference.
Well, what was the difference?
Well, the first place, his muscles wasn't as strong, I can say that for one thing. And then with his age, and then with the false teeth, that pressure. That had a lot to do with it.
Did false teeth bother you much on clarinet?
No way, no way, no way, no way, no way.
Did Bunk play louder or softer in the 20s?
He played louder, he played louder, yeah.
Did he ever play very loud?
Not very loud, no.
But definitely loud?
Definitely louder than he played. Did he have more range or less range? Well, he had more range. More range and he had more execution. It was more fast and more flexible.

Let's see, we were talking about across the lake. Isidore Fritz again, says, those people that aren't living, I mean we like to keep harping on them sometimes because they can't talk for themselves. Was he older much than you? I thought maybe he was an older man when you first heard him.
Yeah, Isidore was an older man than I was.
But then you said he was just learning though too in that band that Bunk taught. I didn't know that before.
He was an older man than I was.
He was older than you.
Yeah. What I'm talking about now when Bunk was teaching that band, that was when I was a boy going back and forth every year.
That's before you really lived over there.

Before I really lived over there. That band moved it on after they left Manneville, they moved it on into Baton Rouge. And they came back to Manneville. And that's where I found out how much a clarinet player Isidore was. Isidore was about one of the best I can say I ever heard. But he never would leave me all in. He never would leave that? I mean he never would come over here to play with me all in. Yeah, he never would come over here.
Why not?
I don't know. He never would come over here. And he played the clarinet, his father played the bass, and the brother Lloyd played the trombone.
He's a dead now of course. He's a dead now, of course.

Yeah, he died in Covington. The last time I saw him I played out that neighborhood with someone. Well he wasn't playing much and he had a lot of work, they were bricklayers. And he was doing contract and work.
Maybe Dan Moody might know the family.
Yeah, probably some of the relatives are still over there.
Yeah, Dan may know the whole family. Well I knew some of the family but because Dan was really not from Manneville, Dan was from Slider.
Are there any musicians left in Mandeville that you know of? I tell you, I don't really know who's left over there.
It's been so long since I've been over there. I don't know who's over there.
When you went across in those days, was that little boat you were going across? Or big boat, whatever it was?
Well it was when I, in those days, first was a camellia. My father used to cook on that. I went over, they had the thing on the top there. Oh yeah, one of those.
Then they had a smaller boat.
What on the top?
The engine, the big shaft.
Yeah, the big shaft.
A walk and boom like thing. Yeah, right in the center.
Rocks back and forth.
That's all it's for me. Did they have a side wheel or a stern wheel off?
No, I think it was two side wheels. Oh.
I think it was two side wheels. Raymond has pictures of it. He played on the boat.
I think Raymond Burke played a little bit. On the chameleon. It must have lasted pretty late then, didn't it?
No, it went out existing and it came back and it didn't stay very long.
And they had the Fairhope, which was a smaller boat. And then they brought in another boat by the name of the Susquehanna. And then they had… Probably Raymond might have played on the Susquehanna.
And the dead rail.
Well I don't remember the dead rail.

Dead rail. Remember that we were speaking of? Yeah. They had the dead dream. What was it like Ms. Zena? I don't know. I never saw it. You never saw it, but you heard it. Oh wow. They had the dead dream.

Another question I just thought of to ask you Ms. Zena, do you remember when you were a girl ever going out to Millenburg to picnics or anything? No, no. I never went. No picnics and things. No kind of picnics in the country or any place? No. You never went? No. What about Spanish Fort? Did you ever go out there to the amusement park? Well, not so long.
I rode there, but I never been to anything there. I'm doing alright.
We can turn it off. We can turn it off. We can turn it off. Talking about the Spanish Fort and then West End, do you remember anything out at West End when you were in the room? No.
No more than when my brother was in Mandelburg working with a, you know, he was a baker. I went to the West End to catch the, the camellia. Eh?
Talk to the thing.

No, it doesn't matter. Talk to anybody more. I went there to catch the, the camellia to go to Mandelburg, but I never been to no picnic or nothing like that there. No. Did you ever hear any brass bands at funerals when you were young? If I ever heard? Yes. Oh, you see. In my day, children didn't go out to everything like the grown people. Did you hear them at all though when you went home?
She heard them. What?

When I, when they'd have a funeral or a, very little parade they had then. Uh huh. But funerals, they'd have with music. Outside of that I don't remember. And that would be, I guess that would be reading music or ear music? Music like they have in the house, the carnet and drums and things like that.
George, you said you think they, they had the bands even a long time ago in the funeral center?
Yeah. Oh yeah, sure they did.
Well did they play a ear when you were a child?
No, most of them were reading bands.
Most of those brass bands were reading.

Well they had a few get together bands, they like, the Labor Day, they have so many bands that they had to send out to countries and get them, you know. Well they'd have a few get together bands that were playing this, the hit stuff like that.
So would they get real ratty in the street? Oh yeah, sure.
They used to call them a tunk band, they'd put them way in the back. What'd they call them? Tunk bands.

You know like hunky tunk. Hunky tunk bands, yeah. Well I wanted to ask too while I met it, Abby played a parade two weeks ago and he was saying over those days, several years ago when you had your little six piece band or something like that, a brass band, you got a lot of more jobs on the street and it sounded good and all too. Did you only use about six or seven pieces in the street at one time or not? No. Abby was talking like you said then the union makes them use ten now.
No, no.
But how big a band when you did have one a few years ago with your name on that drummer, just, we always see that.
Nothing under ten. Nothing under ten. You don't think it was under ten? No.
Eleven.
Ten to twelve, from eleven to twelve the most.
Well how big were the bands when you were a child?

Did you ever count? I never noticed no more than twelve. I never noticed no more than twelve. So times haven't changed too much? No it hasn't changed in that line at all. More than the only change that you find that the bands are not reading, because they had really good brass bands at the time. Because most of them guys that played those few marches weren't no men that played dances, they were just, men you know they played baritone, you don't find no baritone, you don't find no mellophone. No.
What did they have in the band in those days? Say if you had ten pieces or twelve pieces, what was the line of it?

Well they would find two drums, three trumpets, a leaf-like clarinet, and a little mellophone, baritone, the two trombones, and a bass. And the saxes? They didn't have no saxes. They didn't have no saxophone. No sax at all. I never saw no sax.
When did that come in would you say?
Oh, well the first time I played in the band with the saxophone was with, the first man I ever played with in the band was Ed Washington.
Yeah.
And I think that.
Which Ed Washington is that?
Big Ed. Big Ed? Played with, played with Keith Thomas.
Big Ed.
Yeah. He was the first man I ever played with with the saxophone in a band. Because I know when I was in the old Eureka band they didn't have any saxophone at all.
Which was the first band you played in yourself?
The first band in the early 20's. Willie Parker put me in there. And he was, because he was the manager of that band.
That was a Eureka, Willie Parker.
Yeah, that was a Eureka.
And who was in the band? Do you remember anything else?
Well there was an old man, Tito, was playing drum. And there was Cornish playing Tramon.
Slide or Val?

Slide. Playing Slide. And a fellow by the name of Smith was playing Tramon. He was the manager of that band. He died too. And an old fellow by the name of Verrett was playing bass. And Alphonse, I can't call his other name, he was playing, he was a dog fellow, he was a pigeon toe playing the mellophone. And an old man by the name of Tico was playing the baritone. It was Willie Wilson, a fellow by the name of Santimo, and Landry. Big Al Landry. Oh yeah, Andrew Landry.
And on bass drum, let's see who was playing the bass drum.
I can't remember. Willie Parker was playing the bass drum. Who was the snare drummer? Old man by the name of Kato. Oh, Kato. He was a little short, he was a little short. He was old at that time.
In fact, all of them were old men. And what kind of marches did they play?
Almost the same kind of marches they're playing now. Would they be six eights, two fours?
They played nothing but music.
None of them men couldn't play nothing by it. Yeah. More than nothing. Yeah. More than nothing. Yeah.
More than nothing. Yeah. More than nothing.
Well, see, didn't Red Heart say his father was in that band or something?
He played.
I don't remember his father in that band. He must have got in there before I got in there.
That might have been way back.

But yeah, I learned there was another Eureka band in the early days in this band. Probably he was in that band. Might have been in that. But this band here, I'm telling you about this, it's the first time I ever played E-flat clarinet in my life. And we played the second to the last All Fellas Day Parade, which was all day parades. It started at nine o'clock in the morning and lasted five in the evening.
Was that the May the 10th parade? That is, May.

All day, last all day. We used to stop and rest at Espinade and Claiborne, sit in the grass and rest. And they gave a picnic at the fairground and they used a brass band out there and they used a band out in the field, what they called a hunky-tump. Out in the field where a lot of the women were afraid to go out there on account of the guy was grabbing and rake them and the thing out there on the field.
It's pretty rough out there.

Yeah. Well, I used B-flat and I had E-flat clarinet in my pocket. Both of them on the parade, right? Yeah, the first E-flat clarinet I used, Landry was working as a sailor for a drum or a war line, and he got it for me as a trial. And I started playing it and Joe, also Joe Watson, not Watkins the drummer, Joe Watson, Watkins, who was playing with the Sam Morgan band. Well they had a band out, I didn't remember which band he was playing. It was the first time he ever used an E-flat clarinet, it was both of us that day. He couldn't use his and I used mine.
You always did play just Albert's system, I understand.
Just Albert's system.
Did you ever try the Bain system? I tried.
Or bones and people? Yeah, it was a trial once, but I couldn't get it on with it.
Did you know anybody that played that when you were young or any time? No, I didn't know.

I never saw them until the 80 years. I wouldn't say they weren't playing, you know, but I never saw them until the 80 years. Because I get, somewhere or another I get confused. I was in some of those, yeah. But I did have, I had a crown that my mother had got me in the 20s, which was part Albert and part Bim. The bottom part was Bim with the top.
Oh yeah. Professor Minetta told us that some of the fellows used to use in that part. Yeah, my mother got it for me.

How was the tongue? The tongue was good, but one night I was working and it had a silver tube from the, right from where the valve begins coming down, the first half. Yeah. A whole silver tube in there. And all that ones had lost the tone. They just went down one night and I went to use it. And air was too hard, too many air with it. They just lost the tone. I brought it on Bimble between Dolphin and Bourbon. They had a violin maker there. And he was supposed to fix it and I didn't know if something went wrong. He died or something. He got away and I knew he'd get the crown. And it wasn't black. It was color of this, it was brownish.

Oh gosh. Do you think it was made that way, but somebody just got two different parts? The band and the... I don't know. It could have been two different parts. I can't imagine they'd make it ever that way, but probably somebody got two parts.
What was your very first job anyway? Did you ever...
My first job was on a St. Joseph's night, 19 to March. 1914 was my first job.
When 19...
And who was that with?
With a little black eagle band. That was across the lake? Across the lake. I left here to go and play.
Do you remember any of the fellows in the band?

One of them was named, the banjo player was named Walter Lewis, and the drum player was named Broussard. And the trumpet player was named, his name was, he had a French name, Val San. I just remember his first name now, but we used to call him Black Eagle, it was real dark. And I think he died just some years ago in...
They called him the... They called him Black Eagle. That's when the band got the name, I don't know.
But he died in the Tantry, I think, just some years back, he killed a man out there in McCormick, Mississippi.

And he was a trombone player in the band. Yeah, there was a trombone player in the band. And then that was Earl Foster's brother. I think he was with us right now. Earl Foster's brother. I don't know.
He quit playing a long time. And let's see, you had drums, bass, trombone trumpet? Mm-hm.
They had drums, bass, trombone, trumpet?

They had a fellow by the name of Manuel, he was playing bass. The drum player was a people named Bruce Aldo, Burrow, Roosevelt Burrow was a drummer. He had goat hires on the drum, we had that on the goat hires because they couldn't get the hair and the goat hires for the drum.
Did you get paid you say?
Two dollars.
Two dollars in those days? How long would you have to work?
About four in the morning.
You started what time?
Yeah.
Eight to four. Dude, all that's pretty good to pay, wasn't it?
Eight dollars. Yeah, it was a lot of fun out there. A lot of fun.
Did you ever work for really low prices?
I worked for low prices right in the thirties there.
Impression.

I worked for one job, I was just talking to my mother right there. Decatur, not my son, he's bringing me over here. Decatur, Toulouse, Decatur. And then there's a little Shaw Street coming from St. Peter. Wilkinson. Wilkinson. They had a saloon right on that corner. And I worked there one night from eight until four in the morning for six bits.
Which corner was it? Downtown or the uptown?
On the downtown and the uptown side of Bangor, there was a giant right there.
On the downtown? On the lake side. Downtown and the lake side?
On the back of town side, what you call the back of town, and the uptown side. Uptown.
Yeah. That's torn down there. Yeah, it's torn down. A big block.
Little shop right next to that shop. Been there for years. A loading shop. Been there for many, many years.
Yeah, that's right. The same block that I live in. That's right.
And then I worked at the kingfish for two years or something. For a dollar a night. And I never missed a night. Where was the kingfish? Oystin Island and Decatur. Where they sell chickens.
Yeah.

Then I moved from there and I went in the middle of the block to another little place. It was called Mama's Place. And I got a dollar a night there. And I moved further down the block to the Popeye and got a dollar a night there.
Was that every night or just on weekends? Every night. Every night.

Who was playing with you in some of those jumps? Well, the first one I was at Kingfish was Boyd's. Boyd's was playing trumpet. Boyd's Stevens was playing trumpet. Boyd's. And the guy by the name of McGee was playing drum. And Billy, Billy Chase was playing piano. He was on the four of us.
Now McGee, is that, that's Herb Moran?

No, that's not Herb Moran's brother. That's another McGee. That's another McGee. Yeah, he lives in Oakland right now. He was one of the last time I saw him. He quit playing. Used to wear a derby all the time. And then after Boyd's left there, that's where the D came in there. That's where him and Billy got acquainted and got married for. I stood for the wait.
That was all in the 30s then? That was in the 30s.

Who played with you? Then besides that I waited. I was waking there for a dollar a night and Jeanette had been operating on it and I was waiting on the WPA. I'd catch the bus, the truck at 6 o'clock in the morning. I'd get off at 2 in the evening. I'd come in and work from 8.30 to 3 every night. Never miss a night and that's where I got that metal clarinet as well. Oh yeah? I'd buy that metal clarinet.
Where did you get that? You don't have it anymore do you? Yes, I got it. You still got it? I always like that. I got it. I got it. That would be fixed up. I got it. It sounded good, didn't it?
Yeah, I don't know if you get rid of that clarinet.
Well where's he got it though now?
From the Wuerlein. Mr. Voorhees used to work by Wuerlein. They had it there on the exhibition. He used to run that. So it was like a company, $40 something. $40 something actually.
Because I used to see them, I used to see the BAME systems in New York in 1930 were $10 metal metal.
Well this was a brand new home.
I mean you could get them new. Public schools all used in metal, $10. So the Alberts, I didn't know they made them in Alberts as much, but yours is Alberts. One piece was it?
One piece, yeah. The bell comes off and the mouth piece, that's all.
Who worked with you between Toulouse and St. Philip, Decatur, in that joint?
I worked there with, it was three pieces, no it was four pieces. It was Pickett's brother-in-law, he don't play anymore. He was playing saxophone and clarinet.
He was a Santiago?
No, it was another one.
I guess I would find another one.
No, let me see what's his name again. Edward. He works now by Maison Blanche. Can't call around, his name is Edward.
We'll ask Pickett. Yeah, we'll see him someday.

Yeah, Edward, he has a son who plays saxophone now too, he was in school. Edward Johnson, that's what he was named, Edward Johnson. He was playing saxophone, he was a little short, a little old fellow on the art of Chinese, with a little lighter skinned Chinese hair, something just like Chinese. He was playing saxophone. He was playing saxophone. He was playing clarinet. He was playing clarinet. And the old Johnny Brown, when he used to play clarinet, his son, his name is John, instead of Johnny, it's John, it's John. He was playing piano. And Albert Francis was playing drums. Edna Francis, his husband, I know he was a player of that. He was one of the finest drums you had years ago. He played xylophone and everything. His wife was a piano player and it was Edna Francis. She was an alcoholic and she died.
Who did she work with?

Well she worked with different men. She worked a while with the Renny and she worked a while with Arnaud to Pets. She worked with different fellas. Her last job was at Lutchen's with Big I and Winnes Rodgers.

Yeah, I should've seen her. I was wondering about clarinet players again, here to change the subject a little bit. Some of the very first you heard and who were your favorites when you were a boy that you followed in the street? It inspired you. You say you wanted to take up clarinet. Who was the first one you thought was so good that you liked the instrument?

Well Bill, I tell you, in my early days I thought they all were good, those I heard on the street. I know they all couldn't have been as good as I thought they were, but I heard a man like George Bakke, also Charlie McCurtis, T.O. and there was Big I, Louis. Big I, Louis.
How about fixing the coffee, young girl? Fix a little coffee?
Fix you.
Well, I'll drink some if you're going to fix it.
Ordinarily, though, I don't drink much coffee, but there's no trouble.
Yeah, sure.
You mentioned the different clarinetists like T.R.O. and Bachman. You said big eyes.
